lesson.text: Quick memory: a line sits inside REPEAT 3 TIMES, inside REPEAT 2 TIMES. How many times does it run? (2 × 3 = 6 times.) Today: giving a group of steps a name, and using it again.
A procedure is a group of steps with a name. DEFINE square teaches the computer the steps once; after that, the one word square runs them all.
The steps under DEFINE do nothing on their own. They wait until a line calls the procedure by its name. Call it twice, and its steps run twice.
Worked example: this program calls square, moves on 3 with the pen up, and calls square again: two squares. Without the procedure, the square's loop would be written out twice.
Procedures make programs shorter and easier to read. They are easier to fix too: fix a bug inside DEFINE square once, and every square the program draws is fixed.
Give procedures names that say what they do: jump, draw_star, open_gate. A recipe works the same way: 'make the dough' is one step, with its own steps written somewhere else.
Procedures can call other procedures: DEFINE house could call square, then roof. Big programs are built this way, from small named parts (you split big jobs into small ones in grade 3).
Try it in the world: invent a dance with a named move, like spin = turn round, clap, jump. Teach it to a friend, then call it: spin, spin, wave, spin. Next: simulations.

exercises.prompt: The steps under DEFINE run as soon as the program starts, even if nothing calls them.
exercises.hint: What makes a procedure's steps run?
exercises.explain: False: they wait until a line calls the procedure by its name.

choices: a group of steps with a name
a variable that holds a number
a loop that never stops
a kind of robot
exercises.explain: A procedure is a group of steps with a name, like square.

exercises.prompt: How many times does the marked line run?
exercises.hint: The steps under DEFINE run once for each call. Count the calls.
exercises.explain: hop is called 2 times, so JUMP runs 2 times.

exercises.prompt: Match each procedure's name to what it probably does.
exercises.hint: A good name says what the steps do.
exercises.explain: draw_square draws a square, open_gate opens the gate, jump_twice jumps twice and say_hello says hello.

exercises.prompt: How many times does the marked line run?
exercises.hint: Count every call: the ones in the loop and any others.
exercises.explain: The loop calls cheer 3 times, and it is called once more after the loop: 3 + 1 = 4 claps.

exercises.prompt: Which drawing does this program make? The pen starts at the green dot, facing right.
exercises.hint: Draw one step first: along 1, up 1. Then count the calls.
exercises.explain: One step goes along 1 and up 1, and step is called 3 times: a staircase of 3 steps.

exercises.prompt: Why is DEFINE square better than writing the square's steps out 5 times?
exercises.hint: Think about reading the program, and fixing it.
choices: It is shorter, and a bug is fixed in one place
It makes the squares bigger
It makes the computer use more power
It is the only way to draw
exercises.explain: The steps are written once and called 5 times: a shorter program, and one place to fix a bug.

exercises.prompt: Put the steps of making and using a procedure in order.
exercises.hint: You can't call something before it has a name and steps.
items: Choose a name that says what it does
exercises.explain: Name it, DEFINE its steps, call it by name, and its steps run.

exercises.prompt: DEFINE corner: FORWARD 2, TURN LEFT. The program is corner, corner. Which moves does the robot make?
exercises.hint: Write out corner's steps once for every call.
choices: FORWARD 2, TURN LEFT, FORWARD 2, TURN LEFT
FORWARD 2, TURN RIGHT, FORWARD 2, TURN RIGHT
TURN LEFT, FORWARD 2, TURN LEFT, FORWARD 2
FORWARD 3, TURN LEFT, FORWARD 3, TURN LEFT
exercises.explain: Each call of corner is FORWARD 2, TURN LEFT, and there are 2 calls, so the steps come twice. They take the robot to the flag.

exercises.prompt: A bug fixed inside DEFINE square is fixed for every square the program draws.
exercises.hint: Where do the steps of every square come from?
exercises.explain: True: every call runs the same steps from DEFINE square, so one fix mends them all.

exercises.prompt: How many times does the marked line run?
exercises.hint: How many blocks does one call of row place? How many calls?
exercises.explain: Each call of row places 4 blocks, and the loop calls row 3 times: 3 × 4 = 12.

exercises.prompt: How many times does the marked line run?
exercises.hint: Work from the inside out: how many claps in clap3? How many calls of clap3 in song? How many songs?
exercises.explain: clap3 claps 3 times; song calls clap3 twice (6 claps); song is called twice: 2 × 6 = 12 claps.

exercises.prompt: DEFINE house calls square and then roof. Which is true?
exercises.hint: What does a call do, wherever it is written?
choices: house runs the steps of square, then roof
square can only be used once
roof must be written inside house
a procedure can't call another one
exercises.explain: Calling house runs its steps, and those steps call square and roof, so all their steps run in order.

exercises.prompt: A procedure draw_star has 10 lines. Mimi calls it 6 times. Without the procedure she would write its lines out 6 times. How many lines would that be?
exercises.explain: 6 × 10 = 60 lines, instead of the 10 lines written once and 6 short calls.

exercises.prompt: Nothing happens when Bram's program runs. Why?
exercises.hint: Read the call letter by letter and compare it with the name.
choices: He calls jmup, but the procedure is jump
JUMP needs a loop
DEFINE must come last
Procedures can't jump
exercises.explain: The call must match the name exactly. jmup is not jump, so nothing is called.
